title: Can, must, may
goal: Use the modal verbs — *können*, *müssen*, *dürfen*, *wollen* — and build the "bracket" sentence that is German's most distinctive feature.
bekal: express ability, obligation, permission and wanting
put the second verb at the very end of the sentence
ask for something politely (*Können Sie bitte…*)
forbid with *darf nicht*, and say "no need" with *muss nicht*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Die Hausordnung
dialogs.intro: Budi has moved into a new apartment. The caretaker explains the house rules — and almost every sentence he says uses a modal verb.

lines.speaker: Hausmeister:
lines.text: Willkommen! Hier ist die Hausordnung. Können Sie Deutsch lesen?
lines.id: Welcome! Here are the house rules. Can you read German?
lines.literal: welcome! here is the house-rules. can you German read?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ein bisschen. Ich kann noch nicht alles verstehen.

lines.speaker: Hausmeister:
lines.text: Kein Problem. Also: Von 22 Uhr bis 7 Uhr müssen Sie leise sein.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Darf ich am Abend Musik hören?

notes: **The bracket sentence.** The modal verb sits in second position, and the main verb is pushed to the **very end** in its basic form: *Ich **kann** Deutsch **lesen***, *Sie **müssen** den Müll **trennen***. Everything else stands between the two. This is why Germans sometimes have to wait for the last word to know what a sentence actually means.

***nicht müssen* ≠ *nicht dürfen*.** *Sie müssen nicht kommen* = you **don't have to** come. *Sie dürfen nicht kommen* = you **must not** come. The difference is huge, and English speakers fall into a trap here: English "must not" means forbidden, but German *muss nicht* only means "no need".

***können* isn't only about ability.** It's also used for polite requests: *Können Sie mir helfen?*, *Können Sie das wiederholen?* This is much softer than a direct command, and it's what you should use with strangers.

***wollen* is blunt.** *Ich will einen Kaffee* sounds like a demand. For polite wishes use *möchten*, which you met in unit 7. *Wollen* fits a firm intention: *Das will ich lernen* ("I want to learn that").

**Line 3: *müssen Sie leise sein*.** The sentence starts with a time phrase, so the modal verb stays in second position and the subject moves behind it — the unit 10 rule still applies in full. Two rules work together in almost every long German sentence.

***Ruhezeit*** (quiet hours) is a real institution in Germany, not a suggestion: usually 10:00 p.m.–6:00 a.m. every day, plus all of Sunday. Running a washing machine, drilling or playing loud music during those hours can end in a formal letter from the neighbors.

grammars.title: The six modal verbs
body: This group shares two features: the **ich** and **er/sie/es** forms are always identical with no ending, and the vowel changes in all the singular forms.
after: ⚠️ There is no **-t** in the *er/sie/es* form — this is the only verb group in German that works this way. *Er kann*, not *er kannt*. Adding a -t is the easiest beginner mistake to spot.

*Mögen* is different from the other five: it usually is **not** followed by another verb, but takes an object directly. *Ich mag Kaffee* = I like coffee. Its conditional form, *möchte*, you've been using since unit 7.
*Sollen* passes on advice or an order from someone else: *Der Arzt sagt, ich soll mehr schlafen* ("the doctor says I should sleep more"). It also makes offers: *Soll ich helfen?* ("shall I help?").

grammars.title: How the bracket sentence works
body: As soon as there's a modal verb, the sentence has two poles: the modal in second position, the main verb at the end. Everything else goes in the middle.
after: The last row answers a question you may have had since unit 8: when a separable verb meets a modal verb, it **joins back together** and stands whole at the end. *Ich stehe früh auf* → *Ich möchte früh **aufstehen***. Only one verb can occupy the end of the sentence.

**Where *nicht* goes:** to negate the whole sentence, put *nicht* right **before** the verb at the end. *Ich kann heute **nicht** kommen.* If you're negating just one word, *nicht* stands directly in front of that word: *Ich kann **nicht** heute kommen, aber morgen.*

sections.title: Polite sentences that save the day

blocks.text: All of the sentences below are built from *können* and the word *bitte*. Those two ingredients turn a request polite without any advanced grammar.

head: German
English
rows: Could you speak more slowly, please?
Could you write that down, please?
Do I have to do it now?

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note that *bitte* can go almost anywhere in the sentence, but its most natural place is **right after the subject**: *Können Sie **bitte** langsamer sprechen?* Putting it at the end is also correct and sounds a little more pleading.
Practice by changing one and the same sentence with each modal verb. The content stays the same, the meaning changes completely — and that's the fastest way to feel the difference.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: I can (am able to, have time to) work today.
I may (am allowed to) work today.

blocks.title: The three most common mistakes
items: **Forgetting to send the second verb to the end** — *Ich kann sprechen Deutsch*. Correct: *Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.*
**Adding -t to the *er* form** — *Er kannt*, *sie musst*. Correct: *er kann*, *sie muss*.
**Using *nicht müssen* to forbid** — *Du musst nicht rauchen* means "you don't have to smoke", not a ban. The ban is: *Du **darfst** nicht rauchen.*
Ich kann noch nicht alles verstehen.
Darf ich am Abend Musik hören?
Am Sonntag dürfen Sie nicht waschen.
